title: The Shipwrecked Sailor's Return
summary: A young fisherman's boat engine fails far from shore, and he uses his knowledge of currents, stars, and patience to find his way home.
poll: Staying calm is more useful than panicking when something goes wrong.

versions.title: The Shipwrecked Sailor's Return
versions.text:
Salem is a fisherman. He is young. He lives by the sea.

Salem has a boat. It is small.

Each week, he goes out. He goes far out. Fish live far out.

One day, the engine stops. Salem tries to fix it. It will not start.

Salem is scared. He takes a breath. He stays calm. He does not panic.

He thinks of his dad. His dad taught him well. His dad taught him about the current. His dad taught him about the stars.

Salem drops his anchor. He checks the current. It moves one way. It moves home!

Salem lifts the anchor. He lets the boat drift. He uses an oar. He steers with it.

The sun sets. Salem looks up. He sees the stars. The stars show the way.

Back home, his dad waits. Yousef is worried. Salem is not back yet.

The village lights a lamp. It shines out at sea.

Day comes. A man sees a boat. It is Salem!

Salem gets home. He is tired. He is safe and well.

The village is glad. Salem did not give up. He used the current and the stars.

Salem drops his anchor. He wants the boat to stop drifting. He checks which way the current moves. It moves toward his village!

Salem pulls up the anchor. He lets the boat drift with the current. He uses an oar to steer it. When the sun sets, Salem looks up at the stars to check his way.

Back in the village, his father Yousef starts to worry. Salem has not come home by night. The village lights a lamp by the sea so he can find his way.

Early in the morning, someone spots a small boat far out. It is Salem! Slowly, he makes his way home.

The whole village is happy to see him safe. Salem used the current and the stars, and he never gave up.

One afternoon, far from land, the engine stops. Salem checks it. He tries again. It will not start.

At first, Salem feels afraid. But he takes a breath. He stays calm instead. He thinks of his father and his grandfather. They taught him how to read the current. They also taught him how to find his way by the stars.

Salem drops his anchor. This stops the boat from drifting too fast. He watches which way the current moves. He notices something good. The current moves toward his own village!

Salem pulls up the anchor. He lets his boat drift with the current. He uses an oar to steer it the right way. When the sun sets, he watches the stars. They help him check his course.

Back in the village, his father Yousef grows worried. Evening comes, and Salem has not returned. The villagers light a lamp by the harbor. It gives him something to look for in the dark.

Early the next morning, someone spots a small boat far out. It is Salem! Slowly, he makes his way home, tired but safe.

The whole village gathers to welcome him with relief. Salem used the current and the stars instead of panicking, and he never gave up.

versions.title: The Shipwrecked Sailor's Return
versions.text:
Salem is a young fisherman. He lives in a small village beside the sea. His boat is small and wooden. It once belonged to his grandfather.

Each week, Salem sails out to fish, just as his father taught him. He usually travels far from the shore. The best fishing is out where the water is deep and cool.

One afternoon, far from land, the engine suddenly stops working. Salem checks it carefully. He tries again and again. Nothing happens no matter what he does.

At first, Salem feels a flash of fear. He is alone, far from home. But he takes a slow breath and refuses to panic. Instead, he calls to mind what his father and grandfather taught him: how to read the current, and how to find direction by the stars at night.

Salem lowers his anchor so the boat will not drift away too fast. He watches carefully which way the current is pulling. He notices something useful. This current usually flows toward his own village.

Salem pulls the anchor back up. He lets his boat drift slowly with the current, resisting the urge to hurry. He uses an oar to steer, nudging the boat gently back on course. When the sun finally sinks below the horizon, Salem watches the stars appear to check his direction.

Back in the village, his father Yousef grows more worried as the evening passes. Salem has still not returned. The villagers climb to the harbor and light a tall lamp. Somewhere on the dark water, Salem will have a bright light to steer toward.

Early the next morning, someone on the shore finally spots a small boat drifting in from far out on the calm water. It is Salem! Slowly, drifting and paddling, he makes his way home at last, exhausted but unharmed.

The whole village gathers at the shore to welcome him home with great relief. Because Salem used the current and the stars instead of panicking, and because he was patient, he made it back safely.

One particular star, which hardly seems to move across the entire night sky, always points roughly north, and by keeping it consistently on the correct side of his boat, Salem can reasonably anticipate approximately where the unpredictable current will eventually carry him, remaining fairly confident he has not drifted significantly off course even during the most profoundly silent hours of the night.

keyWords.definition: a person who catches fish for a living
keyWords.example: The old fisherman mended his net before sunrise.

keyWords.definition: the machine inside a boat or car that makes it move
keyWords.example: The bus engine made a loud noise before it started.

keyWords.definition: the steady movement of water in one direction
keyWords.example: The current carried the leaf gently down the stream.

keyWords.definition: the small bright lights you see in the night sky
keyWords.example: We counted the stars from the roof of our house.

keyWords.definition: a small group of homes where people live together, smaller than a city
keyWords.example: Everyone in the small village knew each other by name.

questions.stem: What is this story mostly about?
options: A fisherman who builds a new boat
A fisherman whose engine breaks and who finds his way home
A village that moves to a new island
How to ride a camel safely across the hot desert sand
questions.why: The story follows Salem after his engine stops, and how he uses the current and stars to get home.

wrong.A: Salem does not build a new boat in the story.
wrong.C: The village does not move anywhere in the story.
wrong.D: There is no race between boats in the story.

questions.stem: What happens right after Salem's engine stops working?
options: He jumps into the water to swim home
He tries again and again to fix it
He calls his father on a phone
He paddles straight to another boat
questions.why: The story says Salem tries again and again to fix the engine before thinking of another plan.

wrong.A: Salem does not jump into the water in the story.
wrong.C: The story does not mention a phone.
wrong.D: There is no other boat nearby in the story.

questions.stem: Why does Salem drop his anchor after the engine stops?
options: To catch more fish quickly
To stop the boat from drifting too fast while he thinks
To clean the bottom of the boat after a long day of fishing
To signal for help with a loud noise
questions.why: The story says Salem drops his anchor so the boat will not drift away too quickly while he works out a plan.

wrong.A: Dropping the anchor is not about catching fish.
wrong.C: The anchor is not used for cleaning the boat.
wrong.D: The anchor does not make noise to signal for help.

questions.stem: In the story, a current is —
options: a bright star in the sky
a loud sound from the engine
the steady movement of the water
a cold and windy desert night with no moon at all
questions.why: The story shows the current as the moving water that carries Salem's boat toward his village.

wrong.A: A star is in the sky, not the water.
wrong.B: The engine is already broken and silent.
wrong.D: The lamp is a light, not moving water.

questions.stem: How does Salem feel when the engine first stops, and what does he do about it?
options: He feels angry and breaks the oar
He feels scared, but he stays calm instead of panicking
He feels bored and falls asleep in the bottom of the boat
He feels proud and ignores the problem
questions.why: The story says Salem feels scared at first but does not panic, and instead thinks of what his father taught him.

wrong.A: Salem does not break anything in the story.
wrong.C: Salem does not fall asleep; he works out a plan.
wrong.D: Salem does not ignore the problem; he deals with it.

questions.stem: Why is it helpful that the current moves toward Salem's village?
options: He can drift home without paddling the whole way
It means the fish will follow him home
It means the engine will start again on its own
It means the village will come closer to him instead
questions.why: Since the current flows toward his village, Salem can drift with it and only use the oar to steer, saving his strength.

wrong.B: The story does not say fish follow boats home.
wrong.C: The current does not fix the engine.
wrong.D: A village cannot move toward a boat.

questions.stem: Why do the villagers light a lamp by the harbor at night?
options: To celebrate a holiday
To cook the fish that Salem caught earlier that same day
To give Salem a light to steer toward in the dark
To scare away birds from the boats
questions.why: The story says the lamp gives Salem something bright to look for while he is out on the dark water.

wrong.A: The story does not mention a holiday.
wrong.B: The lamp is not used for cooking.
wrong.D: The story does not mention birds.

questions.stem: Why does the author tell us what Salem's father taught him about currents and stars?
options: To explain why Salem is able to find his way home safely
To show that Salem's father is a bad teacher
To describe a different fishing trip from long ago
To explain why the engine broke in the first place
questions.why: Salem's knowledge from his father is exactly what helps him stay calm and get home, which is the point of the story.

wrong.B: The father's teaching helps Salem, showing he taught him well.
wrong.C: The story is about this one trip, not an old one.
wrong.D: Salem's knowledge has nothing to do with why the engine broke.

LOW.prompt: Would you have stayed calm like Salem, or would you have panicked? Explain your answer using at least two facts from the story.
checklist: I clearly said what I think I would do.
I used at least two facts from the story.
I wrote complete sentences with capital letters and periods.
LOW.modelAnswer: I think I would try to stay calm like Salem. In the story, Salem feels scared when the engine stops, but he does not panic. Instead, he remembers what his father taught him about the current and the stars. Because he stayed calm, he was able to drift safely toward his village and get home. I would want to think clearly like that instead of panicking.

keyWords.definition: the line far away where the sky seems to meet the sea or land
keyWords.example: We watched the sun disappear below the horizon.

keyWords.definition: the ability to stay calm and wait without getting upset
keyWords.example: It took patience to wait quietly for the bus in the rain.

keyWords.definition: to move slowly, carried along by water or air rather than by one's own power
keyWords.example: The empty boat began to drift away from the dock.

keyWords.definition: not worried, upset, or excited; peaceful
keyWords.example: She stayed calm even when the lights suddenly went out.

keyWords.definition: a heavy object lowered from a boat to keep it from drifting away
keyWords.example: The sailors dropped the anchor before they went to sleep.

questions.stem: Which sentence best states the central idea of the story?
options: A fisherman spends the whole long afternoon racing another fishing boat all the way back to the busy village harbor
A young fisherman uses patience and knowledge of the sea, instead of panic, to find his way safely home.
A young fisherman builds a brand-new engine for his boat.
A village decides to stop allowing anyone to go fishing alone.
questions.why: The whole story centers on how Salem's calm thinking, knowledge of currents and stars, and patience bring him safely home.

wrong.A: There is no race or second boat in the story.
wrong.C: Salem's engine stays broken; he does not build a new one.
wrong.D: The village does not create any new rule in the story.

questions.stem: What two things does Salem's father teach him that help him later in the story?
options: How to sell fish and how to paint a boat
How to cook the fresh fish and how to mend the torn fishing nets each evening
How to read the current and how to find direction by the stars
How to swim fast and how to build a boat
questions.why: The story says Salem remembers what his father taught him about reading the current and finding direction by the stars.

wrong.A: Selling fish and painting boats are not mentioned in the story.
wrong.B: Cooking and mending nets are not mentioned as the key lessons.
wrong.D: Swimming and building boats are not mentioned as the key lessons.

questions.stem: Why does Salem choose to let the boat drift with the current instead of paddling hard the whole way?
options: He wants to stay out on the water longer to fish
He is waiting for another boat to tow him
How to swim very fast across the bay and how to build a wooden boat from scratch
He knows the current is already carrying him toward his village
questions.why: Because the current naturally flows toward his village, Salem lets it carry the boat and only uses the oar to correct his direction.

wrong.A: Salem is trying to get home, not to fish longer.
wrong.B: No other boat appears to tow him in the story.
wrong.C: Salem is able to use the oar to steer, so he is not too tired to move it.

questions.stem: In the story, the word horizon means —
options: a bright lamp at the harbor
a heavy object that keeps a boat from drifting
a sudden strong wind
the line far away where the sky meets the sea
questions.why: The story describes the sun sinking below the horizon, the far line where the sky meets the sea.

wrong.A: The lamp is a separate object, not the horizon.
wrong.B: That description fits an anchor, not the horizon.
wrong.C: The horizon is not a type of wind.

questions.stem: Why does Salem decide not to panic, based on details in the story?
options: He is certain that another boat is coming to rescue him right away
He has fixed this exact engine before many times
He believes panic rarely solves a problem and can make things worse
He does not understand at first that he could really be in any danger out there
questions.why: The story explains that Salem knows panic rarely solves a real problem and often makes the situation worse, so he chooses to stay calm.

wrong.A: No rescue boat is mentioned as coming for him.
wrong.B: The story does not say he has fixed this engine before.
wrong.D: Salem clearly understands the danger; that is why he feels afraid at first.

questions.stem: What can you infer about Salem's family from how he handles the broken engine?
options: His family lives far away from the sea
His family has taught him a lot about the sea over many years
His family has never been fishing before
His family owns many different kinds of fishing boats docked at the harbor
questions.why: Salem calmly uses detailed knowledge from his father and grandfather, which shows his family has passed down a lot of sea knowledge.

wrong.A: His family clearly lives near the sea, since they are fishers.
wrong.C: His family clearly has fishing experience, since his father and grandfather taught him.
wrong.D: The story only mentions one boat, which belonged to his grandfather.

questions.stem: Why do the villagers light a lamp instead of simply waiting quietly for Salem to return?
options: To warn other boats to stay far away from the harbor
To celebrate that he has already arrived safely
To dry out wet fishing nets more quickly
To actively help guide him home once it gets dark
questions.why: The lamp gives Salem a point of light to steer toward in the dark, which is an active way to help him find his way home.

wrong.A: The lamp is meant to help Salem, not warn boats away.
wrong.B: The villagers do not yet know he has arrived safely when they light it.
wrong.C: The story does not mention drying nets.

questions.stem: How is this story organized?
options: It follows events in order, from the engine breaking to Salem's safe return
It compares two completely different fishing villages side by side in great detail
It explains how to build an anchor step by step
It lists facts about different kinds of fishing boats
questions.why: The story moves through events in time order: the trip, the broken engine, the drift home, and the welcome at the village.

wrong.B: Only one village appears in the story.
wrong.C: The story does not give building instructions.
wrong.D: The story is not a list of facts about boat types.

MID.prompt: Explain how patience helped Salem get home safely. Use at least two details from the story.
checklist: I explained how patience helped Salem.
I used at least two details from the story.
I organized my ideas in a clear order.
MID.modelAnswer: Patience helped Salem get home safely in more than one way. First, instead of panicking when the engine stopped, he stayed calm and thought carefully about what to do. Then, instead of paddling hard and tiring himself out, he patiently let the current slowly carry his boat toward the village, only using the oar to steer. Because he was willing to wait and let the sea do most of the work, he made it home safely instead of exhausting himself for nothing.

keyWords.definition: to find and follow the correct way, especially by boat or plane
keyWords.example: The captain used an old map to navigate through the narrow strait.

keyWords.definition: very careful and paying close attention to small details
keyWords.example: She was meticulous about checking every bolt before the flight.

keyWords.definition: to expect something and prepare for it before it happens
keyWords.example: Good drivers anticipate sudden stops in heavy traffic.
The empty bottle was buoyant enough to stay on the surface.

keyWords.definition: to come together from different directions and meet at one point
keyWords.example: Two busy roads converge at the roundabout near the mall.

questions.stem: Which statement best expresses the central idea of the story?
options: A fisherman competes eagerly against several other local sailors to see who reaches the harbor first
A fisherman survives an engine failure by relying on inherited knowledge of the sea and his own patience, rather than panic.
A fisherman spends months inventing an entirely new and complicated way to build small boat engines from scratch
A village decides that unsupervised fishing alone is far too dangerous and officially bans it
questions.why: The story centers on Salem using knowledge passed down through his family, along with patience, to navigate home safely rather than panicking.

wrong.A: There is no competition with other sailors in the story.
wrong.C: Salem's engine remains broken throughout the story; nothing is invented.
wrong.D: No ban or new rule is mentioned by the village.

questions.stem: Why does the current near the headland prove especially useful to Salem?
options: It is the only place where fish can be caught at all
It is marked clearly with a floating sign that boats can see from very far away each day
It is where two tidal currents converge and happen to flow toward his village
It is the coldest water along the entire coastline
questions.why: The story explains that two tidal currents converge near the headland and flow toward Salem's village, which helps carry his boat home.

wrong.A: The story does not claim fish can only be caught at that one spot.
wrong.B: No floating sign is mentioned anywhere in the story.
wrong.D: The story does not describe the water there as especially cold.

questions.stem: How does Salem use the plastic jug tied to his anchor rope?
options: As a container to store extra drinking water for the long trip home
As a makeshift paddle he uses to steer the boat gently from side to side
As bait he hopes will attract more hungry fish toward the boat
As a buoyant marker that helps him judge the current's speed and direction
questions.why: The story describes Salem tying an empty, buoyant jug to the rope so he can judge the current by watching it bob on the surface.

wrong.A: The jug is empty and used as a float, not for storing water.
wrong.B: Salem uses an oar, not the jug, to steer the boat.
wrong.C: The jug is not described as bait for fish.

questions.stem: In the story, the word meticulous most nearly means —
options: nervous and easily distracted
careless and quick
very careful and attentive to small details
loud, careless, and extremely impatient with everyone around him
questions.why: Salem checks the engine meticulously, meaning he examines it very carefully, trying different things in a methodical way.

wrong.A: Meticulous describes careful attention, not nervousness or distraction.
wrong.B: Meticulous is nearly the opposite of careless.
wrong.D: Being meticulous is about careful attention, not loudness or impatience.

questions.stem: Based on the story, why is Salem able to anticipate roughly where the current will carry his boat?
options: He follows another fishing boat that is traveling the same route as his own boat and crew
He uses the fixed position of a particular star to track his direction over time
He receives updates about the current from a radio on the boat each hour
He simply guesses based on which way the wind is blowing that day
questions.why: By keeping the nearly fixed northern star on the correct side of his boat, Salem can track his direction and anticipate where the current leads him.

wrong.A: No other boat travels alongside Salem in the story.
wrong.C: No radio is mentioned in the story.
wrong.D: The story focuses on the current and stars, not a guess based only on wind.

questions.stem: In what order do these events happen in the story?
options: Salem ties the jug to the rope, the engine stops, the village lights the lamp, Salem drops anchor
Salem drops anchor, the village lights the lamp, the engine stops, Salem ties the jug to the rope
The engine stops, Salem drops anchor, Salem ties the jug to the rope, the village lights the lamp
The village lights the lamp, the engine stops, Salem drops anchor, Salem ties the jug to the rope
questions.why: First the engine fails, then Salem lowers the anchor to think, then he ties the jug to judge the current, and only later, as evening falls, does the village light the lamp.

wrong.A: The jug is tied on after the engine fails, not before it.
wrong.B: The anchor is dropped before the lamp is lit, not after.
wrong.D: The lamp is lit after the engine fails and evening comes, not before.

questions.stem: What can readers infer about panic from how the story describes Salem's reaction to the broken engine?
options: Panic is presented as the fastest and most reliable way to fix a broken boat engine quickly
Panic is presented as a sign of bravery that the story admires
Panic is presented as something only inexperienced fishermen ever feel
Panic is presented as something that usually makes a hard situation worse, not better
questions.why: The story states directly that panic rarely solves a genuine problem and often makes a difficult situation considerably worse, which is why Salem deliberately avoids it.

wrong.A: The story never suggests panic would fix the engine.
wrong.B: The story treats calm thinking, not panic, as admirable.
wrong.C: The story does not say only inexperienced fishermen feel fear or panic.

questions.stem: Why does the author end the story by saying Salem's calm thinking became a story the village would retell for years?
options: To explain why the village later built a bigger harbor
To emphasize the lasting value of knowledge and patience over panic
To suggest that Salem became famous outside the village
To hint that Salem's engine was never actually broken at all
questions.why: By showing the village retelling the story, the author highlights how valuable Salem's calm, knowledgeable response was, reinforcing the story's central lesson.

wrong.A: No bigger harbor is mentioned as being built.
wrong.C: The story only mentions the village, not fame beyond it.
wrong.D: The engine clearly stays broken throughout the whole story.

HIGH.prompt: The poll says staying calm is more useful than panicking when something goes wrong. Do you agree or disagree? Support your argument with evidence from the story about Salem's choices and their results.
checklist: I stated a clear position on the poll statement.
I supported my position with specific evidence from the story.
I addressed at least one point someone might make against my view.
HIGH.modelAnswer: I agree that staying calm is more useful than panicking when something goes wrong. When Salem's engine fails far from shore, he feels afraid but deliberately refuses to panic, because he knows panic rarely solves a real problem and often makes things worse. Instead, his calm thinking lets him use his meticulous knowledge of the current and the stars: he anticipates that the current will carry him toward his village, and he patiently lets it do so instead of exhausting himself. Someone might argue that panic can sometimes push people to act quickly in an emergency, but in Salem's case, quick, frantic action would likely have wasted his energy and left him drifting the wrong way, so his calm, careful approach was clearly the better choice.
